<STATEMENT>
# Problem C — Proof of Impossibility

Time limit: 2 s   Memory limit: 256 MB

The factory has a roster of workers with known conflicting pairs. It is guaranteed that the conflict graph contains at least one set of three workers who pairwise conflict. Any such set proves that two shifts (1 and 2) cannot suffice. Because the assignment is therefore known to be hopeless, your job is not to schedule — it is to certify the impossibility. Output one such set.

## Input
The first line contains two integers n and m (3 ≤ n ≤ 2000,
3 ≤ m ≤ min(n·(n−1)/2, 2·10⁵)).
Each of the next m lines contains two integers u v — a conflicting pair.
It is guaranteed that at least one such triple exists.

## Output
Print three integers a b c on one line with a < b < c such that all three pairs
a–b, a–c, b–c are conflicts. Output the lexicographically smallest such triple
(smallest a; ties by smallest b; then smallest c).

## Example 1
Input:
```
4 5
1 2
1 3
2 3
2 4
3 4
```
Output:
```
1 2 3
```

## Example 2
Input:
```
5 6
1 2
1 4
2 4
3 4
3 5
4 5
```
Output:
```
1 2 4
```
</STATEMENT>
<RATIONALE>
The description was reordered to present the data model (workers and conflicting pairs) and structural guarantees (existence of a conflicting triple) before revealing the objective (certifying impossibility by outputting the triple). This prevents models from pattern-matching the objective in the opening sentence and forces them to read the structural rules first.
</RATIONALE>
<PRESERVED_ANSWER>
The problem still requires finding the lexicographically smallest set of three workers who pairwise conflict, keeping the output identical for all inputs.
</PRESERVED_ANSWER>
<PRESERVED_CLASS>
The underlying computational task remains finding a triangle (K3) in an undirected graph, preserving the original algorithmic complexity.
</PRESERVED_CLASS>
